questions.question: How does npm dependency management work — semver ranges, lockfiles, and node_modules resolution?
questions.title: Npm Semver Deps
questions.direct_answer: package.json declares dependencies with semver ranges: ^1.2.3 allows minor+patch (>=1.2.3 <2.0.0), ~1.2.3 allows patch only, exact pins for no movement. The lockfile (package-lock.json) records the FULL resolved tree — every transitive dep's exact version — making installs reproducible. npm ci installs exactly the lockfile (fails if out of sync — the CI command); npm install updates it. Resolution: nested node_modules per-package for conflicting versions (the reason two copies of a lib can coexist).

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: package.json declares dependencies with semver ranges: ^1.2.3 allows minor+patch (>=1.2.3 <2.0.0), ~1.2.3 allows patch only, exact pins for no movement. The lockfile (package-lock.json) records the FULL resolved tree — every transitive dep's exact version — making installs reproducible. npm ci installs exactly the lockfile (fails if out of sync — the CI command); npm install updates it. Resolution: nested node_modules per-package for conflicting versions (the reason two copies of a lib can coexist).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The semantics, verified:

```
SEMVER: major.minor.patch — breaking.feature.fix
  ^1.2.3  →  >=1.2.3  <2.0.0   (trusts minor/patch — the default)
  ~1.2.3  →  >=1.2.3  <1.3.0   (patch only)
   1.2.3  →  exactly this       (distrust/pin)
  latest  →  whatever publish was latest — the danger zone

LOCKFILE (package-lock.json):
  records the EXACT resolved version of every package in the entire tree,
  including every transitive dependency you never named.
  Commit it. It's what makes 'works on my machine' into 'works everywhere'.

npm ci  vs  npm install:
  ci       — reads the lock EXACTLY, wipes node_modules first, FAILS if
             package.json and lock disagree. The CI/deploy command.
  install  — reconciles; may UPDATE the lock within allowed ranges.
             The dev command.
```

The transitive-dependency reality (why lockfiles exist): you depend on 40 packages; they depend on 2,000. package.json names 40; the lock pins 2,000. Without the lock, tomorrow's install silently picks up new transitive versions — the source of 'nothing changed but the build broke.' The lockfile freezes the entire tree.

The dedupe/nesting model (how conflicts coexist): if two of your deps need different majors of lodash (1.x and 4.x), npm nests — node_modules/depA/node_modules/lodash (1.x) beside top-level node_modules/lodash (4.x). Node's resolution walks UP from the importer until it finds the package — hoisted when versions agree, nested when they don't. This is why 'duplicate package' bugs (two React instances → hooks error) happen and why resolutions/overrides exist to force one copy.

The everyday discipline: commit the lock, use ci in CI, upgrade deliberately (npm outdated → npm update or per-package install @latest → review the diff — a new MAJOR is a migration, not an update), and never edit node_modules to 'fix' something — it's a build artifact.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[package.json: 40 declared + semver ranges] --> I[npm install]
    I --> L[lockfile: 2000 exact versions pinned]
    L --> CI[npm ci: exact tree, fails on drift]
    subgraph resolution
        H[hoisted when versions agree] --> N[nested when majors conflict]
        N --> W[walk up node_modules until found]
    end
    UP[upgrade = explicit event: outdated → bump → review diff → CI]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why semver fails in practice (the honest layer): breaking changes ship in minors (the ecosystem's dirty secret), and 'backward compatible' is judged by the author's imagination, not your usage — you use the one private API edge they changed. The mitigations that matter: lockfiles (the whole tree is frozen, upgrades are explicit events), automated-update PRs with CI (Renovate/Dependabot — each bump becomes a reviewed PR that runs your tests, converting silent drift into a visible gate), and for libraries YOU publish: deprecate before you break, use 0.x to signal instability (0.x minors ARE breaking by convention).

npm vs pnpm vs yarn (the tooling landscape): pnpm solves npm's two real problems — install speed (hard-linked content-addressable store; packages stored once on disk, linked into projects) and the phantom-dependency bug (strict node_modules: you can only import what you declared, because only declared deps are linked at your top level; npm's flat hoisting lets you import undeclared transitive deps that work until a hoist order changes — the bug pnpm exists to kill). Yarn (berry/PnP) pursued the same goals via a different mechanism (no node_modules, a resolver map). The interview-ready summary: all run the same package.json/semver/lockfile model; they differ in disk layout, strictness, and speed.

The audit/supply-chain layer (the 2020s addition): npm audit maps your tree against the advisory database — read it as signal not noise (a dev-dep advisory doesn't ship to users; a prod dep's RCE does). The discipline that matters more than audit scores: lockfiles + CI-install (npm ci) + review of every dependency bump + org-scoped registry policies. Your lockfile is also a security artifact — it's the exact software supply chain you ship, which is why 'commit the lockfile' is both a reproducibility and a security answer.
